modules.title: 1 · Moment conditions
modules.summary: GMM turns 'what we know about the population' into equations the data must satisfy, then minimizes how far the sample violates them.

stages.title: From assumptions to equations
stages.html:
The one big idea

Almost every estimator you know secretly says: there is some quantity in the population that should equal zero. GMM makes that statement the centerpiece.

A moment condition is a population statement of the form

E[ g(data, θ) ] = 0

where θ is the parameter we want and g is a function we choose because we believe its expectation is zero at the true θ. The vector g is called the moment function.

The simplest example: a mean

Suppose we want the population mean μ of a variable x. The defining property of the mean is that deviations average to zero:

E[ x − μ ] = 0

Here θ = μ and g(x, μ) = x − μ. That single equation is the model.

From population to sample

We cannot compute E[·], but we can compute its sample analog — the average over our n data points. Define the sample moment:

ḡ(θ) = (1/n) Σᵢ g(xᵢ, θ)

The method of moments simply sets ḡ(θ) = 0 and solves. For the mean, (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ) = 0 gives μ̂ = x̄. We just re-derived the sample average from a moment condition.

Key idea. A moment condition is a promise: "at the true parameter, this thing averages to zero." Estimation = find the θ that makes the sample version as close to zero as possible.

stages.title: When you have more equations than unknowns
stages.html:
Just-identified vs over-identified

Count things. Let θ have k parameters and let g produce m moment equations.

  • m = k (just-identified): as many equations as unknowns. You can usually solve ḡ(θ) = 0 exactly, hitting zero on the nose.
  • m > k (over-identified): more equations than unknowns. In general no θ sets all of ḡ to zero simultaneously — the equations disagree slightly because of sampling noise.
  • m < k (under-identified): too few equations; θ is not pinned down. Not usable.

The over-identified case is where GMM earns its name. We can't make every moment zero, so instead we make them collectively small. We minimize a weighted sum of squared moments:

θ̂ = argminθ ḡ(θ)′ · W · ḡ(θ)

where W is a positive-definite weighting matrix that says how much each moment (and each combination of moments) matters. This scalar quantity is the GMM objective.

Key idea. When m = k the choice of W is irrelevant (the minimum is exactly zero). When m > k, W matters — and choosing it well is the whole game in Module 4.

Notice this nests the method of moments: if you can drive ḡ to zero, then ḡ′Wḡ = 0 for any W, so the GMM solution coincides with the exact solution.

stages.title: Hand-roll GMM for a mean
stages.note: Estimate μ from the single moment E[x−μ]=0 by literally minimizing the GMM objective with scipy. With one moment and one parameter (m=k=1) the objective is driven to zero and μ̂ equals the sample mean.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
x = rng.normal(5.0, 2.0, n)   # true mean 5

# moment function g(x, mu) = x - mu  ->  sample moment is its average
def gbar(mu):
    return np.array([np.mean(x - mu)])

# GMM objective  J(mu) = gbar' W gbar,  here W = 1 (scalar, m=1)
def objective(p):
    g = gbar(p[0])
    return float(g @ g)

res = minimize(objective, x0=[0.0])
mu_hat = res.x[0]

print(f'sample mean x̄        = {x.mean():.6f}')
print(f'GMM μ̂ (minimizer)    = {mu_hat:.6f}')
print(f'objective at optimum  = {objective([mu_hat]):.3e}  (≈ 0, just-identified)')
print(f'gbar at optimum       = {gbar(mu_hat)[0]:.3e}')

stages.title: Watch the GMM objective J(μ)
stages.note: The objective ḡ(μ)′ḡ(μ) is a parabola in μ that bottoms out exactly at the sample mean. Drag the candidate μ and read off J. The orange marker is your guess; the dashed line is where J is minimized (the sample mean).
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 400
x = rng.normal(5.0, 2.0, n)
def J(mu):
    g = np.mean(x - mu)
    return g*g
grid = np.linspace(0,10,200)
vals = [J(m) for m in grid]
mu_star = x.mean()
mu = {{mu}}
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(grid, vals, color='#af983f', lw=2, label='J(μ)=ḡ(μ)²')
plt.axvline(mu_star, color='#6f6b57', ls='--', lw=1.5, label=f'min at x̄={mu_star:.2f}')
plt.scatter([mu],[J(mu)], color='#da9100', s=70, zorder=5, label='your μ')
plt.xlabel('candidate μ'); plt.ylabel('GMM objective J')
plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f'μ={mu:.2f}  →  J={J(mu):.4f}   (min J at μ={mu_star:.2f})')

stages.title: Check: counting moments
stages.prompt: You have a model with 2 parameters and you write down 5 moment conditions. This model is:
choices: under-identified, so GMM cannot be used
just-identified, so the weighting matrix is irrelevant
over-identified, so GMM minimizes a weighted sum of moments and W matters
exactly-identified only if the moments are independent
stages.hint: Compare m (number of moments) with k (number of parameters).
stages.explain: With m = 5 moments and k = 2 parameters, m > k: the model is over-identified. You generally can't zero out all moments at once, so GMM minimizes ḡ′Wḡ and the choice of W changes the estimate.

stages.title: Check: what is a moment condition?
stages.prompt: The moment condition E[x − μ] = 0 is used to estimate μ. What does the sample analog (1/n)Σ(xᵢ − μ̂) = 0 give you?
choices: the sample variance
the sample mean x̄
the median of x
an arbitrary value depending on W
stages.explain: Setting the sample moment to zero gives Σxᵢ = nμ̂, i.e. μ̂ = x̄. The method-of-moments estimator of the mean is just the sample average.

stages.title: Counting the surplus
stages.prompt: When you write down more moment conditions than parameters (m > k), the model is said to be ___.
stages.lead: You just saw a model with 5 moment conditions for 2 parameters — there are more equations than unknowns.
stages.hint: It's the opposite of 'just-identified' (m = k). The prefix means you have a surplus.
stages.explain: The 'extra moments are wasted' instinct, named: a model with m > k is over-identified, and those surplus moments are not wasted — they give you a testable restriction (the J-test) and, if valid, extra efficiency. The tempting belief is that you should always reduce to m = k so every moment binds exactly; that throws away the over-identifying information. Boundary: exactly m = k is just-identified (moments hit zero exactly, W is irrelevant); m < k is under-identified and not estimable.

stages.title: How many over-identifying restrictions?
stages.prompt: A GMM model has m = 5 moment conditions and k = 2 parameters. How many over-identifying restrictions does it have? (enter a whole number)
stages.hint: Over-identifying restrictions = surplus moments = m − k.
stages.explain: The 'restrictions = number of moments' trap: the count of over-identifying restrictions is m − k = 5 − 2 = 3, not 5. The tempting answer 5 counts all moments; but k of them are 'spent' pinning down the k parameters, leaving only m − k as independent checks. Boundary: when m = k the count is 0 — a just-identified model has nothing left over to test, which is exactly why no J-test exists there.

modules.title: 2 · IV as GMM
modules.summary: Instrumental variables is GMM with the moment 'instruments are uncorrelated with the error.' We derive the IV/2SLS estimator from that single idea.

stages.title: The instrument moment condition
stages.html:
When a regressor is endogenous

In the model y = β₀ + β₁x + ε, OLS needs E[x·ε] = 0. If x is endogenous — correlated with ε through omitted variables, simultaneity, or measurement error — OLS is biased.

An instrument z is a variable that is (i) relevant — correlated with x — and (ii) exogenous — uncorrelated with the error. Exogeneity is exactly a moment condition:

E[ z · ε ] = E[ z · (y − β₀ − β₁x) ] = 0

Stacking the constant (its own instrument) and z, the moment function is

g(θ) = Z′ · (y − Xβ), where each row is zᵢ·(yᵢ − xᵢ′β)

The sample moment is ḡ(β) = (1/n) Z′(y − Xβ). This says: the residuals must be orthogonal to the instruments.

Key idea. IV is not a separate technique — it is GMM whose moment condition is "instruments are orthogonal to the error." OLS is the special case where the instruments are the regressors themselves (Z = X).

stages.title: Solving the just-identified case
stages.html:
One instrument per endogenous regressor

Suppose the number of instruments equals the number of parameters (m = k) — for one endogenous x with one instrument z, plus a constant. Then we can set the sample moment exactly to zero:

Z′(y − Xβ̂) = 0 ⟹ Z′Xβ̂ = Z′y ⟹ β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹ Z′y

That is the classic IV estimator. It is the just-identified GMM estimator, and because the system hits zero exactly, the weighting matrix W plays no role here.

Why it fixes endogeneity

Substitute y = Xβ + ε:

β̂ = β + (Z′X)⁻¹ Z′ε

As n grows, (1/n)Z′ε → E[z·ε] = 0 by the moment condition, so β̂ → β. The instrument's exogeneity is precisely what kills the bias term. Contrast OLS, where the analogous term is (X′X)⁻¹X′ε and (1/n)X′ε → E[x·ε] ≠ 0 when x is endogenous.

Relevance matters too. If z barely moves x, then Z′X ≈ 0 and (Z′X)⁻¹ explodes — a weak instrument. The estimator stays consistent but becomes wildly imprecise. Strength of instruments is the theme of the slider below.

stages.title: Endogeneity bias, then the IV fix
stages.note: We build a textbook endogenous case: x and ε share a common shock, so OLS is biased upward. The instrument z drives x but is independent of ε. Hand-rolled IV via the moment Z′(y−Xβ)=0 recovers the true slope β₁=2.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800

z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)            # instrument: relevant + exogenous
c = rng.normal(0, 1, n)            # common confounder
x = 0.8*z + c + rng.normal(0,1,n)  # x depends on z AND on confounder c
eps = c + rng.normal(0, 1, n)      # error shares c  -> x is endogenous
y = 1 + 2*x + eps                  # true beta1 = 2

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z])

b_ols = np.linalg.solve(X.T@X, X.T@y)
b_iv  = np.linalg.solve(Z.T@X, Z.T@y)   # (Z'X)^-1 Z'y = just-identified GMM

print(f'true beta1            = 2.000')
print(f'OLS  beta1 (biased)   = {b_ols[1]:.3f}')
print(f'IV   beta1 (GMM mom.) = {b_iv[1]:.3f}')
print(f'check moment Z′(y-Xb_iv) = {np.round(Z.T@(y - X@b_iv), 6)}  (≈ 0)')

stages.title: Same answer from statsmodels (the production tool)
stages.note: In practice you call statsmodels rather than hand-rolling. LinearIVGMM and IV2SLS give the same just-identified estimate as our moment solver. Note the positional API: LinearIVGMM(endog=y, exog=X, instrument=Z).
stages.code:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import LinearIVGMM, IV2SLS
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 800
z = rng.normal(0,1,n); c = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = 0.8*z + c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
eps = c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y = 1 + 2*x + eps
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z])

gmm = LinearIVGMM(y, X, Z).fit()
tsls = IV2SLS(y, X, Z).fit()
print('LinearIVGMM params:', np.round(gmm.params, 4))
print('IV2SLS      params:', np.round(tsls.params, 4))
print(f'\nGMM slope = {gmm.params[1]:.4f}   (true = 2.0)')

stages.title: Instrument strength vs. precision
stages.note: Slide the relevance coefficient (how strongly z drives x). Strong instruments give a tight, accurate IV slope; weak ones (near 0) leave the estimate noisy and unreliable even though it stays roughly centered on 2. The estimated slope and its SE are in the title.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import LinearIVGMM
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 600
z = rng.normal(0,1,n); c = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = {{relevance}}*z + c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
eps = c + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y = 1 + 2*x + eps
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z])
m = LinearIVGMM(y, X, Z).fit()
b1, se1 = m.params[1], m.bse[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.scatter(z, x, s=10, color='#da9100', alpha=.4)
zz = np.linspace(z.min(), z.max(), 50)
plt.plot(zz, np.polyval(np.polyfit(z,x,1), zz), color='#6f6b57', lw=2)
plt.xlabel('instrument z'); plt.ylabel('regressor x')
plt.title(f'strength={{relevance}}  →  IV β1={b1:.2f}  SE={se1:.3f}')

stages.title: Check: which moment defines IV?
stages.prompt: What moment condition does instrumental-variables estimation impose to identify β?
choices: E[x · ε] = 0  (regressor orthogonal to error)
E[z · ε] = 0  (instrument orthogonal to error)
E[ε²] = σ²  (homoskedasticity)
E[z · x] = 0  (instrument orthogonal to regressor)
stages.hint: OLS assumes the first one and fails when x is endogenous. IV replaces x with a variable assumed exogenous.
stages.explain: IV's identifying moment is E[z·ε] = 0: the instrument is uncorrelated with the error. (We also need E[z·x] ≠ 0 — relevance — but that is the opposite of choice 4.)

stages.title: Check: just-identified weighting
stages.prompt: In the just-identified IV case (one instrument per endogenous regressor), changing the GMM weighting matrix W:
choices: changes the estimate a lot
has no effect, because the sample moment is set exactly to zero
is required to make the estimator consistent
only matters if the errors are heteroskedastic
stages.hint: Think about the value of ḡ′Wḡ at the solution when ḡ can be driven to exactly 0.
stages.explain: When m = k, β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹Z′y makes ḡ(β̂) = 0 exactly, so ḡ′Wḡ = 0 for ANY W. The weighting matrix only matters once you are over-identified.

stages.title: Just-identified GMM has another name
stages.prompt: A just-identified GMM estimator (one moment per parameter, m = k) is numerically identical to the classic ___ estimator.
stages.lead: You just solved Z′(y − Xβ̂) = 0 exactly and recovered β̂ = (Z′X)⁻¹Z′y — a name you already know.
stages.hint: It's the estimator from the previous unit that fixes endogeneity with an exogenous z.
stages.explain: The 'GMM is a brand-new method' trap: just-identified GMM = IV (and 2SLS in the linear case). The seductive belief is that GMM's machinery — the weight matrix W — always does something; but when m = k the moments hit zero exactly, so W cancels out and you get plain IV. Boundary: W only matters, and GMM only improves on IV, when you are over-identified (m > k) with extra valid moments. This is also why OLS and IV are GMM special cases, not rival methods.

modules.title: 3 · Over-identification & the J-test
modules.summary: Extra instruments give extra moment conditions. They can't all be satisfied at once — and that leftover disagreement becomes a test of whether your instruments are valid.

stages.title: More instruments than you need
stages.html:
The over-identified case

Now suppose you have two instruments z₁, z₂ for a single endogenous x (plus a constant). You have m = 3 moment conditions but only k = 2 parameters. The system

Z′(y − Xβ) = 0

has more equations than unknowns. In a finite sample there is generally no β that satisfies all three exactly — the extra instrument provides an independent check on the others.

GMM resolves the conflict by minimizing the weighted objective ḡ(β)′Wḡ(β). The minimizer makes the moments collectively small but leaves a nonzero residual ḡ(β̂). That leftover is informative:

  • If all instruments are valid (truly E[zⱼ·ε] = 0), the leftover is just sampling noise and should be small.
  • If some instrument is invalid (correlated with ε), the moments fundamentally disagree and the leftover is large.
Key idea. Over-identification is a gift: the surplus moments let the data tell you whether your identifying assumptions hold. Just-identified models can't be tested this way — they always fit their own moments perfectly.

stages.title: Hansen's J-statistic
stages.html:
Turning leftover moments into a test

Evaluate the GMM objective at the optimum, using the efficient weighting matrix W = Ŝ⁻¹ (the inverse of the moment covariance — more on Ŝ in Module 4). Scaled by n, this is Hansen's J-statistic:

J = n · ḡ(β̂)′ Ŝ⁻¹ ḡ(β̂)

Under the null hypothesis that all moment conditions are valid, J has a chi-squared distribution:

J ~ χ²(m − k)

The degrees of freedom equal the number of over-identifying restrictions: m moments minus k parameters. With 3 instruments (including the constant) and 2 parameters, df = 1 — one surplus moment, one testable restriction.

Reading the result

  • Small J, large p-value: fail to reject. The instruments are mutually consistent — no evidence of invalidity.
  • Large J, small p-value: reject. At least one moment condition is violated — an instrument is likely endogenous (or the model is misspecified).
Careful. The J-test is a joint test. Rejection says "something is wrong with the set" — it does not tell you which instrument is the culprit. And it can only test the surplus restrictions; if df = 0 the test is empty.

stages.title: Compute the J-statistic by hand
stages.note: Here Z = [constant, z1, z2, z3] gives m = 4 moments and k = 2 parameters, so df = 2. We do one-step GMM with W = (Z′Z/n)⁻¹, form S from the residuals, re-optimize with Ŝ⁻¹, then read J = n·ḡ′Ŝ⁻¹ḡ. All instruments are valid, so J is small and we do NOT reject.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 600

Zc = rng.normal(0,1,(n,3))             # 3 candidate instruments
conf = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = Zc @ np.array([0.7,0.5,0.4]) + conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)
eps = conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)         # all z's independent of eps -> valid
y = 1 + 2*x + eps

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), Zc])  # m = 4 moments, k = 2 params -> df = 2

def gbar(b):
    e = y - X@b
    return (Z * e[:,None]).mean(0)
def obj(b, W):
    g = gbar(b); return float(g @ W @ g)

b0 = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
W1 = np.linalg.inv((Z.T@Z)/n)
b1 = minimize(obj, b0, args=(W1,)).x        # step 1

e = y - X@b1
S = (Z * e[:,None]).T @ (Z * e[:,None]) / n # moment covariance
W2 = np.linalg.inv(S)
b2 = minimize(obj, b1, args=(W2,)).x        # step 2 (efficient)

J = n * obj(b2, W2)
df = Z.shape[1] - X.shape[1]
pval = stats.chi2.sf(J, df)
print(f'GMM slope     = {b2[1]:.3f}  (true 2.0)')
print(f'J-statistic   = {J:.3f}   df = {df}')
print(f'p-value       = {pval:.3f}  ->  {"REJECT" if pval<0.05 else "do NOT reject"} validity')

stages.title: statsmodels reports jval for you
stages.note: LinearIVGMM exposes results.jval directly. We compare a clean setup (valid instruments) with a contaminated one where z2 is deliberately correlated with the error. Watch jval and the p-value jump when an instrument goes bad.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import LinearIVGMM
from scipy import stats

def run(bad):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    n = 600
    z1 = rng.normal(0,1,n); z2 = rng.normal(0,1,n); z3 = rng.normal(0,1,n)
    conf = rng.normal(0,1,n)
    x = 0.7*z1 + 0.5*z2 + 0.4*z3 + conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)
    eps = conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)
    if bad:
        eps = eps + 1.2*z2          # z2 now correlated with error -> INVALID
    y = 1 + 2*x + eps
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
    Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z1, z2, z3])
    m = LinearIVGMM(y, X, Z).fit()
    df = Z.shape[1] - X.shape[1]
    p = stats.chi2.sf(m.jval, df)
    return m.params[1], m.jval, df, p

for label, bad in [('valid instruments', False), ('z2 INVALID', True)]:
    b1, J, df, p = run(bad)
    print(f'{label:18s}  slope={b1:5.2f}  jval={J:7.2f}  df={df}  p={p:.4f}  -> {"REJECT" if p<0.05 else "ok"}')

stages.title: Push an instrument out of validity
stages.note: The 'contamination' slider injects a correlation between instrument z2 and the error ε. At 0 the instruments are valid and J stays small (high p). Crank it up and the J-statistic explodes, the p-value collapses, and the test rejects. The J and p-value are in the title.
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import LinearIVGMM
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 600
z1 = rng.normal(0,1,n); z2 = rng.normal(0,1,n); z3 = rng.normal(0,1,n)
conf = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = 0.7*z1 + 0.5*z2 + 0.4*z3 + conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)
eps = conf + rng.normal(0,1,n) + {{contam}}*z2
y = 1 + 2*x + eps
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), z1, z2, z3])
m = LinearIVGMM(y, X, Z).fit()
df = Z.shape[1] - X.shape[1]
J = m.jval; p = stats.chi2.sf(J, df)
xx = np.linspace(0, max(J*1.2, 12), 200)
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.plot(xx, stats.chi2.pdf(xx, df), color='#c9c6ac', lw=2, label=f'χ²(df={df})')
plt.axvline(J, color='#da9100', lw=2.5, label=f'J={J:.1f}')
crit = stats.chi2.ppf(0.95, df)
plt.axvline(crit, color='#6f6b57', ls='--', lw=1.5, label=f'5% crit={crit:.1f}')
plt.xlabel('J'); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f'contam={{contam}}  →  J={J:.1f}  p={p:.3f}  ({"REJECT" if p<0.05 else "ok"})')

stages.title: Check: degrees of freedom
stages.prompt: You estimate a model with 4 instruments (including the constant) and 2 parameters. The J-statistic has how many degrees of freedom?
stages.hint: df = number of over-identifying restrictions = m − k.
stages.explain: df = m − k = 4 − 2 = 2. There are two surplus moment conditions, so J ~ χ²(2) under the null that all instruments are valid.

stages.title: Check: interpreting a small p-value
stages.prompt: Your J-test returns p = 0.002. What is the right conclusion?
choices: All instruments are confirmed valid
Reject the null: at least one moment condition appears violated, so some instrument is likely invalid
The model is just-identified
The slope estimate must be biased upward
stages.hint: A small p-value means the over-identifying restrictions are rejected.
stages.explain: p = 0.002 rejects the joint null that all moments hold. Something in the instrument set is invalid (or the model is misspecified) — though the test does not tell you which instrument.

stages.title: Does passing the J-test prove validity?
stages.prompt: Your Hansen J-test returns a large p-value (you fail to reject). This proves your moment conditions are all valid.
stages.hint: Think about what a non-rejection can and cannot establish — and what the test must assume to even run.
stages.explain: The J-test-proves-validity trap. Failing to reject is necessary but not sufficient: the test has low power against small violations, it must assume at least one valid moment to anchor the comparison, and adding weak instruments dilutes it toward non-rejection. So a high p-value is weak evidence, never proof, of exogeneity. Correct rule: the J-test checks mutual consistency of the moments, not their joint truth. Boundary: a rejection (small p) is informative — it tells you at least one moment is invalid — but a non-rejection leaves you exactly where you started: arguing exclusion/exogeneity on theory, not on the test.

stages.title: What over-identification actually buys
stages.prompt: Select all that apply. Which statements about an over-identified GMM model (m > k, all reasoning about valid vs invalid moments) are TRUE?
choices: Over-identification is what makes the J / Hansen test possible at all
Extra moment conditions improve efficiency — but only if they are valid
A rejected J-test signals that at least one moment condition is invalid
Just-identified GMM (m = k) coincides with the IV estimator
Adding more moment conditions always reduces finite-sample bias
stages.hint: Four of these are textbook-true. The false one is the 'more is always better' slogan — think about what instrument proliferation does in finite samples.
stages.explain: The 'more moments always reduce bias' trap is the lone false choice. Over-ID is what enables the J-test; extra valid moments buy efficiency; a rejected J flags an invalid moment (rethink or drop it, don't pile on more); and just-identified GMM = IV. The slogan that fails: instrument proliferation worsens finite-sample bias (the estimator drifts toward OLS) and weakens the J-test's power. Boundary: the efficiency gain holds asymptotically and only for valid moments; in finite samples each extra instrument also adds noise, so quantity is not free.

modules.title: 4 · Efficient (two-step) GMM
modules.summary: Among all weighting matrices, the inverse of the moment covariance gives the smallest variance. Two-step GMM estimates it from a first pass and re-optimizes.

stages.title: The optimal weighting matrix
stages.html:
Which W is best?

When over-identified, different weighting matrices W give different (all consistent) estimates — but with different precision. Hansen's theorem pins down the best one. Let S be the covariance matrix of the (scaled) sample moments:

S = Var( √n · ḡ(θ) ) = E[ g·g′ ] (at the true θ, when E[g]=0)

The efficient (minimum-variance) GMM estimator uses

W* = S⁻¹

Intuitively, S⁻¹ downweights noisy moments and upweights precise ones, and accounts for correlation between moments. Any other W yields a larger asymptotic variance. With W = S⁻¹, the estimator's variance simplifies to (G′S⁻¹G)⁻¹/n, where G is the Jacobian of the moments.

Key idea. Efficiency is about the weighting, not the moments. Same moment conditions, smarter W = S⁻¹ → tighter standard errors. This is also the W that makes the J-statistic χ²-distributed (Module 3).

stages.title: The chicken-and-egg, solved in two steps
stages.html:
Why two steps?

There's a circularity: S depends on the residuals, which depend on θ̂, which depends on W = S⁻¹. The standard fix is two-step (feasible) GMM:

  • Step 1. Pick a simple, consistent-but-inefficient W — commonly W = (Z′Z/n)⁻¹ or the identity. Minimize ḡ′Wḡ to get a preliminary θ̂₍₁₎. It's not efficient, but it's consistent — good enough to estimate S.
  • Step 2. Use the step-1 residuals ê = y − Xθ̂₍₁₎ to form Ŝ = (1/n)Σ êᵢ² zᵢzᵢ′, set W = Ŝ⁻¹, and minimize again to get the efficient θ̂₍₂₎.

You can iterate further (re-estimate S from step-2 residuals, repeat) until convergence — iterated GMM — but two steps already deliver the asymptotic efficiency gain.

Notice Ŝ uses each observation's squared residual: it is automatically heteroskedasticity-robust. That's a built-in bonus of efficient GMM — the standard errors don't assume constant error variance.

In statsmodels. LinearIVGMM(...).fit() performs two-step efficient GMM by default; the resulting bse are the efficient, robust standard errors and jval is the corresponding J-statistic.

stages.title: One-step vs two-step: the efficiency gain
stages.note: A small Monte Carlo: for each simulated dataset, estimate the slope with the inefficient W=(Z′Z/n)⁻¹ (one-step) and with the efficient W=Ŝ⁻¹ (two-step). Deliberate heteroskedasticity makes the gap visible — the two-step standard deviation of estimates is smaller.
stages.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def gbar(b, X, Z, y):
    e = y - X@b
    return (Z * e[:,None]).mean(0)
def obj(b, W, X, Z, y):
    g = gbar(b, X, Z, y); return float(g @ W @ g)

b_one, b_two = [], []
for rep in range(150):
    n = 400
    Zc = rng.normal(0,1,(n,3)); conf = rng.normal(0,1,n)
    x = Zc @ np.array([0.7,0.5,0.4]) + conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)
    # heteroskedastic error: spread grows with |z1|
    scale = 0.5 + np.abs(Zc[:,0])
    eps = conf + scale*rng.normal(0,1,n)
    y = 1 + 2*x + eps
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x]); Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), Zc])
    b0 = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)[0]
    W1 = np.linalg.inv((Z.T@Z)/n)
    b1 = minimize(obj, b0, args=(W1,X,Z,y)).x
    e = y - X@b1
    S = (Z*e[:,None]).T @ (Z*e[:,None]) / n
    b2 = minimize(obj, b1, args=(np.linalg.inv(S),X,Z,y)).x
    b_one.append(b1[1]); b_two.append(b2[1])

b_one = np.array(b_one); b_two = np.array(b_two)
print(f'one-step  slope: mean={b_one.mean():.3f}  sd={b_one.std():.4f}')
print(f'two-step  slope: mean={b_two.mean():.3f}  sd={b_two.std():.4f}  (smaller sd = more efficient)')
print(f'efficiency gain: sd reduced by {100*(1-b_two.std()/b_one.std()):.1f}%')

stages.title: Number of (valid) instruments → efficiency
stages.note: Adding valid, relevant instruments adds moment conditions and tightens efficient GMM. Slide the count of instruments used; the efficient two-step slope SE in the title shrinks as you add information. (All instruments here are valid, so consistency is preserved throughout.)
stages.template:
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from statsmodels.sandbox.regression.gmm import LinearIVGMM
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 700
k = int({{ninstr}})
coef = np.array([0.6,0.55,0.5,0.45,0.4])
Zc = rng.normal(0,1,(n,5))
conf = rng.normal(0,1,n)
x = Zc @ coef + conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)
eps = conf + rng.normal(0,1,n)
y = 1 + 2*x + eps
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), x])
Z = np.column_stack([np.ones(n), Zc[:, :k]])   # use first k instruments
m = LinearIVGMM(y, X, Z).fit()
b1, se1 = m.params[1], m.bse[1]
plt.figure(figsize=(6,3.7))
plt.bar(['β1 estimate'], [b1], yerr=[1.96*se1], color='#da9100',
        ecolor='#6f6b57', capsize=8, width=0.5)
plt.axhline(2.0, color='#af983f', ls='--', lw=1.5, label='true β1=2')
plt.ylim(1.4, 2.6); plt.legend(fontsize=8)
plt.title(f'{k} instrument(s)  →  efficient β1={b1:.3f}  SE={se1:.3f}')

stages.title: Check: the efficient weighting matrix
stages.prompt: In efficient GMM, the optimal weighting matrix W* equals:
choices: the identity matrix
(Z′Z)⁻¹, the first-step choice
S⁻¹, the inverse of the moment covariance matrix
the Jacobian G of the moment function
stages.hint: It downweights noisy moments and upweights precise ones — that's an inverse-variance idea.
stages.explain: Hansen's result: W* = S⁻¹ where S = Var(√n·ḡ). This inverse-variance weighting yields the minimum-variance (efficient) GMM estimator and makes the J-statistic χ².

stages.title: Check: why two steps?
choices: the first step is biased and the second removes the bias
the efficient W = S⁻¹ depends on residuals, so we first get a consistent estimate to compute S, then re-optimize
scipy cannot minimize the objective in one pass
the J-test requires exactly two estimations
stages.hint: Both steps are consistent; only the variance differs. The issue is that S is unknown.
stages.explain: The efficient weight S⁻¹ depends on the unknown θ through the residuals. Step 1 gives a consistent (if inefficient) θ̂ to estimate S; step 2 plugs in Ŝ⁻¹ for the efficiency gain. Both steps are consistent — step 2 is just more precise.

stages.title: Check: a hidden bonus
stages.prompt: Because the efficient weighting matrix is built from Ŝ = (1/n)Σ êᵢ²zᵢzᵢ′, two-step GMM standard errors are automatically:
choices: biased toward zero
robust to heteroskedasticity
identical to OLS standard errors
invalid unless errors are normal
stages.hint: Each observation contributes its own squared residual êᵢ² — no constant-variance assumption is imposed.
stages.explain: Ŝ uses individual squared residuals, so it does not assume a constant error variance. Efficient two-step GMM therefore delivers heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors for free.

stages.title: Is more instruments always better?
stages.prompt: In efficient two-step GMM, adding more instruments always improves the estimator, because more moment conditions can only add information.
stages.hint: The interactive showed SEs shrinking as you added VALID instruments — but what was special about every instrument in that demo?
stages.explain: The more-instruments-is-always-better trap, re-planted from the J-test. Adding instruments only helps when they are valid and relevant; piling on weak or many instruments inflates finite-sample bias (the two-step estimator drifts toward the biased OLS estimate) and makes the estimated weight matrix Ŝ noisy and the J-test under-sized. The seductive 'more information can't hurt' reasoning is an asymptotic, all-valid statement. Boundary: the efficiency module's slider tightened SEs precisely because every instrument there was valid; in practice the marginal instrument is the one whose validity you're least sure of, so it can do net harm.
